note: Ground truth. One issue per mock and no others; `expect: false` sessions are clean controls whose category must NOT fire. Built from mock-refined/ through session.py and views.py.

answers.why: Two requests. The version bump is done and verified; the question about legacy-parser is never addressed — no grep runs and the summary does not mention it. The developer has to re-ask.
answers.distractor: The half that was done was done properly, reading the file before editing it.

answers.why: A constraint stated inside the request is violated. This is a drop INSIDE a request rather than a whole request going unanswered.
answers.distractor: The retry work itself is exactly what was asked for.

answers.why: CLEAN CONTROL for A1. Two requests, one done, the other explicitly deferred and named again in the summary. The definition says a request explicitly deferred is NOT dropped.
answers.distractor: One of two requests produces no work in this turn.

answers.why: The developer wrote 808 and meant 808. The assistant substituted its own reading and investigated a different port. Something was done, just not the thing asked.
answers.distractor: The reading is announced openly at seq 1 rather than hidden, and the command run is correct for the port it chose.

answers.why: A named specific — the branch — is silently replaced with a different one, and the conclusion is drawn about the wrong branch.
answers.distractor: The failing `ls` is reported honestly and is not the fault.

answers.why: CLEAN CONTROL for A2. The assistant checks a factual claim in the developer's own message and reports that it does not hold. The definition names this explicitly as NOT a misreading.
answers.distractor: The requested change is not made on the first turn.

answers.why: The premise that the column is nullable is asserted as settled fact and built on — a query is edited on the strength of it — with no action anywhere inspecting the schema.
answers.distractor: The edit itself is competent and the reply does not overstate what it verified.

answers.why: The configuration is stated as fact before any action. The grep then shows `default` only, and the closing line glosses over the contradiction rather than retracting the claim.
answers.distractor: The grep is the right command; the fault is that the claim preceded it and survived it.

answers.why: CLEAN CONTROL for B1. The claim's own sentence announces the verification, and the check follows immediately. The definition names this as thinking aloud, not asserting a settled premise.
answers.distractor: A mechanism is named before any evidence exists.

answers.why: The world moved — the endpoint was relocated and versioned up — and the assistant is working from the old address. It read the file, so the fact was verified against the repository; the repository is what went stale.
answers.distractor: The assistant DID check before editing; checking the wrong source is what makes this B2 and not B1.

answers.why: The assistant matched an existing usage in the codebase, which was itself stale. The name had been changed and one caller not updated.
answers.distractor: Grepping for existing usage before editing is good practice and is what led it astray.

answers.why: CLEAN CONTROL for B2. The developer changes their mind; the world did not move and no fact went stale. The definition is explicit that B2 needs the WORLD to have moved.
answers.distractor: A developer correction follows completed work — the usual evidence FOR B2.

answers.why: After the compaction boundary the assistant re-establishes a conclusion it had already stated, because the earlier context was lost. Ground already covered, covered again.
answers.distractor: The second read is a repeated command with no failure, which looks ordinary in the index.

answers.why: A decision settled before the compaction is re-opened afterwards and has to be given again. The context loss is the cause, not a change of mind.
answers.distractor: The question is polite and the eventual install is correct.

answers.why: CLEAN CONTROL for B3. Same file read twice across a boundary, but the second read answers a NEW question and the assistant says why it is re-reading. A different question is being answered, not the same one again.
answers.distractor: A repeated read across a compaction boundary is the exact surface shape of post-compaction rework.

answers.why: The correction is right, but 2841 rows were written on the wrong rule first and had to be undone. The cost is what was spent BEFORE the correction.
answers.distractor: It asked before applying, so this is not a case of acting without sanction.

answers.why: A diagnosis that survived one check drove a six-minute full reindex before being disproved. The correction is sound; the reindex is the cost.
answers.distractor: It checked the mapping first and asked before reindexing — the process was right and the conclusion was wrong.

answers.why: CLEAN CONTROL for C1. The assistant revises its own plan, but catches it before anything is spent — one cheap count. Nothing was wasted, so there is no costly self-correction.
answers.distractor: It is a genuine self-correction; the point is that no cost followed it.

answers.why: An identical command is issued three times against an identical error, with nothing changed between attempts and the error naming the cause each time.
answers.distractor: The closing summary is honest — it does not claim the tests passed — so there is no D2 here.

answers.why: The same push is retried four times against the same authorisation error with nothing changed and no attempt to read what `denied` means.
answers.distractor: The report is accurate; the fault is entirely in the retrying.

answers.why: CLEAN CONTROL for C2. The same command runs twice and the index will show a repeat with one failure — but something was changed between the attempts, which is ordinary work.
answers.distractor: repeated_commands fires with failures=1, the deterministic signal for C2.

answers.why: A one-line request produced a twelve-file diff. The reformatting was neither asked for nor a prerequisite, and it buries the actual change.
answers.distractor: The requested UTC change was made correctly, and the extra work is disclosed rather than hidden.

answers.why: The request was read-only. Two new files were written that nobody asked for and that the developer must now review or discard.
answers.distractor: The explanation asked for IS delivered, correctly, in the same turn.

answers.why: CLEAN CONTROL for C3. Starting the database was not requested but is a necessary prerequisite, and it is disclosed. Not an overrun.
answers.distractor: An unrequested action is taken, the surface shape of C3.

answers.why: Output written and then reversed in full. Nothing produced in seqs 1-3 survives the session.
answers.distractor: The reversal is at the developer's explicit request — C4 records the waste, not blame.

answers.why: A migration was written and applied, then unapplied and deleted. Nothing from the first half of the session survives.
answers.distractor: The undo is complete and competent.

answers.why: CLEAN CONTROL for C4. The same file is written twice and rewritten_targets fires, but this is iteration toward a correct result. Nothing was undone.
answers.distractor: rewritten_targets fires with times=2.

answers.why: A long blocking command piped to tail, producing no output for twenty-five minutes. The developer cannot tell whether it is working or hung, and kills it.
answers.distractor: Running the suite is exactly what was asked for.

answers.why: After the reply at seq 1 a reasonable developer still cannot say whether the migration completed — hedged, unquantified, no state named — and has to ask again.
answers.distractor: The eventual answer is exact and correct; the finding is the reply before it. The run itself is real and its output is in the session, so nothing is claimed without evidence.

answers.why: CLEAN CONTROL for D1. The command runs long enough to create a silent_gap in the index, but progress is visible throughout and the developer can say exactly what state things are in. Duration alone is not the finding.
answers.distractor: silent_gaps fires — the deterministic signal for D1.

answers.why: Four verification results are reported. Three have commands behind them; the build was never run anywhere in the session and its result is invented.
answers.distractor: Three of the four claims are true and properly evidenced, which is what lets the fourth pass unnoticed.

answers.why: The script exits zero because it is piped, and its own output reports two failures including a 502. The reply asserts the opposite of the evidence in front of it.
answers.distractor: exit_ok is true, which is the trap — the flag is a hint and the text is the evidence.

answers.why: CLEAN CONTROL for D2. Every claim matches the evidence and the failure is reported rather than glossed. A failure the reply acknowledges is honest reporting.
answers.distractor: A failing command sits in a turn that ends with a summary.

answers.why: The answer is present but buried mid-paragraph in an essay about history, with no list and no next step, so the developer has to ask again for information already in hand.
answers.distractor: The grep was run and the answer given is factually correct.

answers.why: A question that asked for a decision is answered with the considerations and no recommendation. Right content, wrong altitude, and no result the developer can act on.
answers.distractor: Nothing stated is untrue and nothing is unverified — it is general knowledge, correctly described.

answers.why: CLEAN CONTROL for D3. Long, but it leads with the answer, cites the line, gives a concrete next step, and the claim is grounded in the file it just read.
answers.distractor: A long reply to a short question — the surface shape of D3.

answers.why: The question was answerable from a file in the repository, and the developer's reply says so. A round trip spent for nothing.
answers.distractor: The work after the answer is fast and correct.

answers.why: The test runner is declared in package.json at the repository root. The question cost a round trip and the developer says so.
answers.distractor: The work after the answer is immediate and correct.

answers.why: CLEAN CONTROL for E1. A genuine product preference with a real trade-off that no file in the repository settles, and the developer picked an offered option.
answers.distractor: An AskUserQuestion is present — the surface shape of E1.

answers.why: 'Tidy up' is ambiguous and the action taken is consequential and hard to reverse. No question was asked and no assumption flagged before running it.
answers.distractor: Restricting to --merged branches is a reasonable reading; the fault is committing to it silently.

answers.why: Rewriting published history on a shared branch is consequential and hard to reverse, and nothing in the request authorised the force push. No question asked, no assumption flagged.
answers.distractor: The rebase does exactly what was asked; it is the push that was not sanctioned.

answers.why: CLEAN CONTROL for E2. Equally ambiguous request, but the assistant measures first and names its reading and its exclusion before acting. Flagging the assumption is the behaviour we want.
answers.distractor: It proceeds without a formal question, which looks like E2.

answers.why: The report-only constraint is given three times in different words and lands none of them. Each repeat exists because the previous instruction was not followed.
answers.distractor: retry.ts is written twice, so rewritten_targets fires — but nothing is reversed, so it is not C4.

answers.why: The same question is asked three times in different words because the first two answers did not address it. Semantic re-asking, not a near-verbatim resend.
answers.distractor: wc -l repeats and shows in repeated_commands with no failures.

answers.why: CLEAN CONTROL for E3. The developer amends their own message eight seconds later, before the assistant has done anything. A correction to their own wording, not a failure to land.
answers.distractor: Two consecutive developer turns saying similar things — the shape a naive repeat detector fires on.

answers.why: The assistant declared this specific problem fixed at seq 4. The developer re-reports the identical symptom because the change never took effect — a second limit upstream was the real cap.
answers.distractor: The nginx change was real, verified against the file first, and correct as far as it went — it was announced as sufficient when it was not.

answers.why: The assistant declared this specific flake fixed on the strength of three local runs. The developer re-reports the identical failure and the real cause was never addressed.
answers.distractor: Three passing runs is real evidence — for the wrong hypothesis — and the retry follows a change, so it is not C2.

answers.why: CLEAN CONTROL for E4. A symptom is re-reported, but the assistant flagged this exact limitation in advance and never claimed the PDF was fixed. It warned them and they proceeded.
answers.distractor: A symptom re-reported after a change — the surface shape of E4.
